subject: biology
title: Glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle
key_idea: Aerobic respiration oxidises glucose in four stages. Glycolysis in the cytoplasm makes pyruvate. The link reaction and Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix remove carbon dioxide and load coenzymes with hydrogen. The coenzymes then pass the hydrogen to the electron transport chain.

blocks.text: Every living cell respires to make ATP. Plants, animals and microorganisms all need energy, because living processes cannot happen without it.

items: Active transport uses ATP to move substances against their concentration gradient, for example mineral ions into root hair cells.
Movement uses ATP, for example in muscle contraction and in cilia and flagella.
Anabolic (building) reactions use ATP, for example in DNA replication and protein synthesis.
Maintaining body temperature in mammals and birds uses energy released by respiration.
Respiration makes ATP, which supplies energy for cell processes.
Active transport, movement and anabolic reactions all need ATP.
Plants respire as well as photosynthesise.

blocks.text: The mitochondrion is the site of the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Its structure suits these jobs.

diagram.alt: An explorer of the parts of a mitochondrion. Tap each part to read its job.
diagram.prompt: Tap a part of the mitochondrion to see what it does

parts.name: Outer membrane
parts.detail: A smooth, partially permeable membrane around the organelle. It separates the mitochondrion from the cytoplasm.

parts.name: Intermembrane space
parts.detail: The narrow gap between the two membranes. Protons are pumped into it, so a proton gradient builds up.

parts.name: Inner membrane
parts.detail: Folded and impermeable to protons. It holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, and it is the site of oxidative phosphorylation.

parts.name: Cristae
parts.detail: Folds of the inner membrane. They give a large surface area for electron carriers and ATP synthase.

parts.name: Matrix
parts.detail: The fluid inside the inner membrane. It holds the enzymes of the link reaction and Krebs cycle, and it is the site of both.

parts.name: Mitochondrial DNA
parts.detail: A loop of DNA in the matrix, with ribosomes, so the mitochondrion can make some of its own proteins.

items: Matrix: link reaction and Krebs cycle.
Inner membrane and cristae: electron transport chain and ATP synthase.
Cristae give a large surface area for ATP production.

blocks.text: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm. It does not need oxygen, so it is the first stage of both aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

items.text: Glucose (6C) is phosphorylated using 2 ATP, making hexose bisphosphate (fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, 6C). This makes it more reactive and traps it in the cell.
The hexose bisphosphate splits into two molecules of triose phosphate (3C).
Each triose phosphate is oxidised by removing hydrogen, which is accepted by NAD to make reduced NAD.
Each triose phosphate is converted to pyruvate (3C), making 2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.

items: Net yield per glucose: 2 ATP (4 made, 2 used), 2 reduced NAD and 2 pyruvate.
Glycolysis occurs whether or not oxygen is present.
Glycolysis is in the cytoplasm and is anaerobic.
Glucose is phosphorylated, split into two triose phosphates, then oxidised to pyruvate.
Net: 2 ATP, 2 reduced NAD and 2 pyruvate per glucose.

blocks.text: When oxygen is available, pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix by active transport. The link reaction then converts it to acetyl coenzyme A.

items: Pyruvate (3C) is decarboxylated: carbon dioxide is removed.
Pyruvate is also dehydrogenated (oxidised): hydrogen is removed and NAD is reduced to reduced NAD.
The remaining acetate (2C) combines with coenzyme A to make acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl CoA).
Coenzyme A carries the acetyl group to the Krebs cycle.
It happens twice per glucose, once for each pyruvate.
Pyruvate → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + reduced NAD.
Coenzyme A transfers acetyl (2C) groups to the Krebs cycle.
Occurs in the matrix, and no ATP is made.

blocks.text: The Krebs cycle takes place in the matrix. It is a cycle of reactions, each catalysed by a specific enzyme.

items.text: The acetyl group (2C) from acetyl CoA combines with oxaloacetate (4C) to make citrate (6C). Coenzyme A is released and used again.
Citrate loses two carbon atoms as CO₂ in a series of steps.
Hydrogen is removed from intermediates and accepted by NAD and FAD, making reduced NAD and reduced FAD.
One ATP is made by substrate-level phosphorylation.
The 4C molecule is regenerated so the cycle can continue.

rows: 4 CO₂, 6 reduced NAD, 2 reduced FAD, 2 ATP

items: Acetyl (2C) + oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate (6C).
Each turn: 2 CO₂, 3 reduced NAD, 1 reduced FAD and 1 ATP.
The cycle runs twice per glucose.

blocks.text: Coenzymes are small molecules that carry groups between enzymes. Three are needed in respiration.

items.meaning: Accepts hydrogen from glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle, becoming reduced NAD.
Accepts hydrogen in the Krebs cycle, becoming reduced FAD.
Carries acetyl (2C) groups from the link reaction into the Krebs cycle.
Removal of a carbon dioxide molecule from a compound.
Removal of hydrogen from a compound, which oxidises it.
Making ATP by transferring a phosphate group directly from another molecule to ADP.

items: Reduced NAD and reduced FAD take hydrogen to the inner mitochondrial membrane.
There they pass hydrogen to carriers in the electron transport chain, which makes most of the ATP.
This also regenerates NAD and FAD, so glycolysis and the Krebs cycle can continue.

checks.q: State where glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle occur in a eukaryotic cell.
checks.a: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle occur in the mitochondrial matrix.

checks.q: Describe what happens to pyruvate in the link reaction.
checks.a: Pyruvate is decarboxylated (CO₂ removed) and dehydrogenated (NAD reduced to reduced NAD). The 2C acetate combines with coenzyme A to make acetyl coenzyme A.

checks.q: Explain the importance of decarboxylation, dehydrogenation and reduced coenzymes in the Krebs cycle.
checks.a: Decarboxylation removes carbon from the substrate as CO₂, so citrate (6C) is converted back to oxaloacetate (4C). Dehydrogenation removes hydrogen, which is accepted by NAD and FAD to make reduced NAD and reduced FAD. These carry hydrogen to the electron transport chain, where most ATP is made.

items: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix by active transport.
Acetyl coenzyme A reacts with a four-carbon molecule, releasing coenzyme A and producing a six-carbon molecule that enters the Krebs cycle.
In a series of oxidation-reduction reactions the Krebs cycle generates reduced coenzymes and ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, and carbon dioxide is lost.
Other respiratory substrates include the breakdown products of lipids and amino acids, which enter the Krebs cycle.
Required practical 9: investigate the effect of a named variable on the rate of respiration of cultures of single-celled organisms, such as yeast.

Overall reaction of aerobic respiration: the respiratory substrate is split to release carbon dioxide as a waste product, and hydrogen is joined with atmospheric oxygen to release a large amount of energy.
Respiration is a many-stepped process. Each step is controlled and catalysed by a specific intracellular enzyme, so energy is released in small amounts.

Glycolysis: phosphorylation of hexoses, and the production of ATP, reduced coenzyme and pyruvate. Pyruvate becomes lactate in anaerobic conditions. Details of intermediate stages and compounds are not required.
